title: Supervised vs Unsupervised: Choosing the Right Paradigm
description: A retail company has a dataset of 2 million customer transactions with no manually assigned labels. They want to identify natural groupings in customer purchasing behaviour to inform marketing strategy. Which learning paradigm applies?
options: Supervised learning, because the transaction history acts as implicit labels for each customer
Unsupervised learning, because the goal is to discover structure without predefined target labels
Reinforcement learning, because the system learns from feedback on each marketing campaign
Semi-supervised learning, because some customers have responded to past campaigns and others have not
explanation:
This is unsupervised learning. The defining feature of unsupervised learning is the absence of a target variable — the algorithm must find structure in the data on its own. Customer segmentation from raw transactions, with no predefined 'correct' groupings, is a canonical unsupervised use case (typically k-means or hierarchical clustering).

Option A is wrong: transaction history is input data, not a label. A label would be something like 'churned' or 'high-value customer' that a human has assigned. Without that, you have no target to predict.

Option C is wrong: reinforcement learning requires an agent that takes actions and receives reward signals over time. A batch of historical transactions with no feedback loop is not a reinforcement learning setting.

Option D is wrong: semi-supervised learning uses a small amount of labelled data alongside a large unlabelled pool. The question specifies no labels at all — not 'very few labels'.
hints: Ask yourself: does the dataset contain a column that represents the 'right answer' the model should learn to predict?
If there is no target variable — no column a human has labelled — the only option is to find structure the data itself reveals.

title: Supervised vs Unsupervised: Fraud Detection Setup
description: A payments company has 5 years of transaction records. A fraud team has manually reviewed and labelled 80,000 of them as 'fraud' or 'legitimate'. They want to build a model that flags new incoming transactions in real time. Which paradigm applies, and why?
options: Unsupervised learning, because fraud patterns constantly evolve and labels become stale
Supervised learning, because there is a labelled dataset with a known target outcome to learn from
Unsupervised learning, because the model must generalise to fraud types it has never seen before
Reinforcement learning, because the model should improve from feedback when a flagged transaction is confirmed or cleared
explanation:
This is supervised learning. The team has a labelled dataset — each transaction is marked 'fraud' or 'legitimate' — and the goal is to predict that label for new transactions. The existence of a target variable (the label) and a training set with known outcomes is the hallmark of supervised learning.

Option A is wrong: label staleness is a real operational concern (concept drift), but it doesn't change the paradigm. You still train on labelled data; you manage drift by retraining periodically.

Option C is wrong: generalising to unseen fraud types is a challenge for any model, but it doesn't define the paradigm. A supervised model trained on historical fraud labels can still be deployed to flag new transactions — it just may not catch entirely novel attack vectors.

Option D is wrong: while a feedback loop could be added later as an enhancement, the setup described is a standard batch-trained supervised classifier. Reinforcement learning would require defining a reward function and an agent acting in an environment, which isn't described here.
hints: The key question is whether a target variable exists in the training data.
If a human has explicitly assigned a label to each training example, you have the defining ingredient of supervised learning.

title: Diagnosing Overfitting from Train-Validation Gap
description: A model trained on a 100,000-row dataset achieves 96% accuracy on the training set and 71% accuracy on a held-out validation set. The validation set was not used during training. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: The model is underfitting — it has not learned enough from the training data
The model is overfitting — it has memorised the training data and fails to generalise
The validation set is too small to produce reliable accuracy estimates
The model needs more training epochs to close the gap
explanation:
A large gap between high training accuracy (96%) and low validation accuracy (71%) is the textbook signature of overfitting. The model has learned patterns specific to the training examples — including noise and coincidental correlations — rather than the underlying signal that generalises to new data.

Option A is wrong: underfitting produces poor performance on both training and validation sets. If a model were underfitting, training accuracy would also be low (e.g. 70%), not 96%.

Option C is wrong: while validation set size matters, the question states the held-out set is from a 100,000-row dataset, which is more than sufficient for reliable estimates. The 25-point gap is too large to attribute to sampling noise alone.

Option D is wrong: training longer typically worsens overfitting. The model is already memorising training data — adding more epochs will not help it generalise. The correct remedy is regularisation, more training data, or a simpler model.
hints: Compare the two accuracy numbers: what does a large gap between training performance and validation performance tell you about what the model has learned?
A model that performs well on data it trained on but poorly on data it has not seen has memorised rather than learned.

title: Recognising Underfitting
description: You train a linear regression model to predict house prices from 15 features including size, location, and age. The model achieves an R² of 0.41 on the training set and 0.39 on the validation set. A colleague suggests the model needs more regularisation. What is the actual problem?
options: Overfitting — the small gap between train and validation R² confirms the model generalises poorly
Underfitting — both scores are low and nearly identical, suggesting the model lacks capacity to capture the signal
Data leakage — the validation R² being close to training R² means the sets overlap
Overfitting — more regularisation would reduce the training R² further and bring it closer to validation R²
explanation:
When both training and validation performance are poor and nearly equal, the model is underfitting — it lacks the capacity or flexibility to capture the underlying patterns. A linear model on 15 features may be too simple for house price prediction, which has non-linear relationships between features.

Option A is wrong: a small gap between train and validation scores is the sign of good generalisation, not poor generalisation. Overfitting produces a large gap, not a small one.

Option C is wrong: data leakage would typically cause the validation score to be artificially high (because future information leaked into training), not merely close to training score. Close scores are normal and expected — they indicate the model generalises consistently, even if poorly.

Option D is wrong: more regularisation would constrain the model further, making underfitting worse. Regularisation is the solution to overfitting; applying it to an already-underfitting model would make both scores worse.
hints: Look at both scores together: when training performance itself is poor, the model has not yet captured the signal in the training data.
A small train-validation gap means the model generalises consistently — the problem is the absolute level of performance, not the gap.

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Model Complexity
description: You are choosing between three models for a regression problem. Model A (linear regression) has high training error and high validation error. Model B (polynomial degree 10) has near-zero training error and very high validation error. Model C (polynomial degree 3) has moderate training error and moderate validation error that closely tracks training error. Which model best represents the bias-variance sweet spot?
options: Model A — the consistent performance across training and validation means it has low variance
Model B — near-zero training error means the model has learned the data perfectly
Model C — moderate error on both sets with a small gap indicates balanced bias and variance
Model A — because simpler models always generalise better than complex ones
explanation:
Model C is at the sweet spot. It has moderate error (not too high, which would indicate underfitting/high bias) and a small gap between training and validation error (not too large, which would indicate overfitting/high variance). This is the classic picture of a well-calibrated model.

Model A has high bias: the consistent but high error on both sets means it cannot capture the signal in the data. Yes, its variance is low, but low variance at the cost of high bias is not useful — the model is simply wrong.

Model B has high variance: near-zero training error with very high validation error is the signature of a model that has memorised the training data, including its noise. It will not generalise.

Option D is wrong as a general rule: simpler models are not always better. There is a point of minimum total error where adding complexity helps more than it hurts. The right complexity depends on the data, not a blanket rule.
hints: The sweet spot is where total error — not just training error — is minimised. Think about what each type of error tells you.
A small gap between training and validation error is desirable. But the absolute level of error on both also matters.

title: Data Splitting: Purpose of the Test Set
description: A team trains a model, evaluates it on the validation set, tunes hyperparameters, re-trains, and repeats this cycle 40 times. They then evaluate the final model on the test set and report that number as their model's real-world performance estimate. What is the problem with this approach?
options: Nothing — the test set was never used during training, so the estimate is unbiased
The test set estimate is biased because repeated validation-based selection implicitly optimises for the validation distribution, not the test distribution
The model should have been evaluated on the test set after each iteration to track progress
The validation set should have been used as the test set to maximise the data available for final evaluation
explanation:
The test set estimate is compromised. Even though the test set was never directly used, the 40-iteration process used validation performance as the selection criterion. By picking the best-performing configuration across 40 tries, the team has implicitly overfit to the validation set — and the model selected may have simply gotten lucky on the validation distribution rather than being genuinely better.

The test set is supposed to be a proxy for truly unseen data. If decisions (including 'which hyperparameters to use') were made using the validation set, the test set remains the only honest estimate. But if you cycle through many configurations using validation, then the final test set evaluation still gives an inflated estimate because model selection was informed by validation performance and the test set was chosen as the final gate — not an independent sample.

Option A is wrong: the test set not being seen during training is necessary but not sufficient. The selection process can still bias the final estimate even without direct test set contact.

Option C is wrong: evaluating on the test set repeatedly would make it worse, not better — that directly leaks test set information into model selection.

Option D is wrong: the validation set has a different purpose (tuning) than the test set (unbiased final evaluation). Merging them would destroy the ability to do either correctly.
hints: Think about what the 40-iteration selection process is really doing: across all those choices, which set is the model implicitly being optimised for?
The test set provides an unbiased estimate only if no decisions — including which model to deploy — were made based on test set performance.

title: Data Splitting: Temporal Ordering
description: You are building a model to predict next-month customer churn using 3 years of subscription data. A colleague proposes a random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split. What is the primary risk with this approach?
options: The split percentages are wrong — a 70/15/15 split is more appropriate for time-series data
Random splitting allows future data to appear in the training set, introducing temporal data leakage
Random splitting produces a validation set that is too small to detect overfitting reliably
The model will not be able to learn seasonal patterns if the data is randomly shuffled
explanation:
The core problem is temporal data leakage. With random splitting, rows from month 30 of the dataset might land in training while rows from month 6 land in validation. The model then 'learns' from future information — future customer behaviour, economic conditions, or feature distributions — when predicting the past. This produces an unrealistically optimistic estimate of performance.

For any time-series or temporal dataset, splits must respect the time ordering: training on months 1–24, validating on months 25–30, testing on months 31–36 (for example). The model should never see data from the future relative to any given training example.

Option A is wrong: the exact percentages (80/10/10 vs 70/15/15) are secondary concerns. The ordering violation is the structural problem.

Option C is wrong: 10% of a 3-year dataset is likely thousands of rows — sufficient for reliable estimates. The sampling error from a 10% validation set is not the primary risk here.

Option D is wrong: seasonal patterns are a concern but a secondary one. Shuffling does disrupt sequence-based learning, but the fundamental issue is the leakage of future information into training, which biases all learned patterns.
hints: What does it mean for a model to 'see the future'? Think about which rows might end up in training when you shuffle a time-ordered dataset.
Any split strategy for temporal data must ensure that every training example predates every validation example, and every validation example predates every test example.

title: Feature Scaling: When It Matters
description: You are training two models on the same dataset: a k-nearest neighbours classifier and a decision tree classifier. The features have very different scales — one feature ranges 0–1 and another ranges 0–100,000. For which model is feature scaling critical, and why?
options: Both models equally — all ML algorithms are sensitive to feature scale because gradient-based optimisation converges faster when features are normalised
Decision tree only — trees use feature thresholds that are sensitive to the absolute scale of each feature
K-nearest neighbours only — KNN uses distance metrics where large-scale features dominate the calculation
Neither model — modern implementations automatically normalise features internally before fitting
explanation:
KNN relies on distance calculations between data points (e.g. Euclidean distance). A feature with range 0–100,000 will contribute 100,000× more to the distance than a feature with range 0–1, effectively making that single feature dominate all nearest-neighbour decisions. Without scaling, KNN is essentially using only the large-scale feature.

Decision trees, by contrast, make binary splits on individual features at a time: 'is feature X > threshold?' The threshold is chosen within the feature's own distribution, so whether it ranges 0–1 or 0–100,000 does not change which split is optimal relative to the other features. Trees are scale-invariant.

Option A is wrong: gradient descent does benefit from feature scaling (faster convergence), but decision trees do not use gradient descent. The statement is incorrect as a blanket claim.

Option B is wrong: this reverses the truth. It is KNN, not decision trees, that is sensitive to scale.

Option D is wrong: no standard implementation of KNN auto-normalises. This is an explicit preprocessing step the practitioner must apply.
hints: Think about what each algorithm actually computes: one computes distances between points, the other computes comparisons against thresholds within a feature.
For distance-based algorithms, ask: if one feature is 100,000× larger, what happens to its contribution to the distance calculation?

title: Feature Scaling: Normalisation vs Standardisation
description: A dataset contains a 'salary' feature with values ranging from $20,000 to $500,000 and several known outliers above $1,000,000. You want to scale this feature before feeding it to a logistic regression model. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Min-max normalisation — it maps all values to [0, 1] and is always preferred for neural networks and logistic regression
Standardisation (z-score) — it is less affected by outliers than min-max and preserves the relative spread of the distribution
Min-max normalisation — because logistic regression requires all inputs to be strictly bounded between 0 and 1
No scaling is needed — logistic regression learns coefficient weights that inherently account for feature scale differences
explanation:
Standardisation (subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation) is more robust when outliers are present. Min-max normalisation maps the entire range to [0, 1] using the minimum and maximum values — if there are outliers at $1M+, those become the maximum and compress the meaningful range of values ($20K–$500K) into a tiny portion of [0, 1], making the feature nearly useless.

Standardisation is bounded by the distribution's standard deviation, so outliers shift the mean and inflate the std dev slightly but do not compress the majority of values into a corner of the scale.

Option A is wrong: while min-max is common for neural networks (especially with sigmoid/tanh activations), it is not universally preferred and is specifically problematic in the presence of outliers.

Option C is wrong: logistic regression does not require inputs to be in [0, 1]. The model applies weights and a sigmoid activation at the output, not the input. This is a common misconception.

Option D is wrong: logistic regression is sensitive to feature scale because gradient descent converges more slowly when features have very different scales. An unscaled salary feature will dominate the optimisation relative to a binary 0/1 feature.
hints: Think about what an outlier at the maximum does to min-max scaling: where does it push the values that are not outliers?
Standardisation uses distributional statistics (mean, std dev) rather than extremes (min, max), making it more resistant to values far from the bulk of the data.

title: Cross-Validation: Purpose and Motivation
description: A data scientist trains a model on 80% of their data and evaluates it on the remaining 20%. A colleague argues they should use 5-fold cross-validation instead. What is the primary advantage cross-validation provides that a single train/validation split does not?
options: Cross-validation uses more data for training because each fold uses 80% of the data across all iterations
Cross-validation provides a performance estimate that is less sensitive to the particular random split chosen, by averaging across multiple held-out sets
Cross-validation prevents overfitting by ensuring the model never sees the same data twice
Cross-validation is faster than a single split because the model is trained on smaller subsets of data
explanation:
The primary advantage of k-fold cross-validation is variance reduction in the performance estimate. A single random split might accidentally place easy or hard examples disproportionately in the validation set, producing an unusually optimistic or pessimistic estimate. By averaging performance across k different held-out sets, cross-validation produces an estimate that is more representative of the model's true generalisation performance.

Option A is partially true but not the primary advantage. Each fold does use k-1/k of the data for training, but the key benefit is reliability of the estimate, not the amount of training data.

Option C is wrong: cross-validation does not prevent overfitting in itself. A model trained with cross-validation can still overfit to the training folds. Cross-validation is an evaluation strategy, not a regularisation technique.

Option D is wrong: cross-validation is slower, not faster. It requires training k separate models instead of one. The computational cost is roughly k× that of a single split.
hints: If you ran the same 80/20 split five different times with different random seeds, how much would your performance estimate vary? Cross-validation addresses that variance.
Think of cross-validation as averaging k performance estimates instead of relying on one — what property of averages is being exploited?

title: Classification Metrics: Precision vs Recall
description: A medical imaging model detects tumours in X-rays. It flags 120 images as positive; 90 of those are true tumours and 30 are false alarms. Of the 200 actual tumours in the dataset, 110 are missed by the model. In this clinical context, which metric should be prioritised and why?
options: Precision — minimising false alarms is most important because unnecessary follow-up procedures cause patient harm
Recall — missing a real tumour (false negative) is more costly than an unnecessary follow-up (false positive) in a cancer screening context
F1 score — it equally balances precision and recall and is the correct metric whenever both types of error matter
Accuracy — it captures the model's overall correctness across all images, including non-tumour cases
explanation:
In cancer screening, the asymmetry of error costs strongly favours recall. Missing a tumour (false negative) means a patient goes untreated and the cancer may progress — a potentially fatal outcome. A false positive leads to further tests, which is costly and stressful but manageable. The model in this question has recall of 90/200 = 45%, meaning it misses 55% of real tumours. That is the primary concern.

Precision here is 90/120 = 75%, meaning 25% of flagged cases are false alarms. In a screening context, these are followed up with further imaging — expensive and inconvenient, but not as harmful as the alternative.

Option A is wrong: while false alarms have real costs, in screening for life-threatening conditions, the cost of a missed case outweighs the cost of an unnecessary follow-up.

Option C is wrong: F1 is appropriate when precision and recall are equally important. Here they are not — the domain dictates that recall is more important.

Option D is wrong: accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced. If 95% of X-rays are negative, a model that flags nothing achieves 95% accuracy while catching zero tumours.
hints: Think about the consequences of each type of error in this domain: what happens to a patient if the model misses their tumour versus flags a healthy image?
Recall measures: of all actual positives, how many did the model find? Precision measures: of all flagged positives, how many were real?

title: ROC-AUC: Interpreting the Curve
description: A binary classifier achieves an AUC-ROC score of 0.50 on a held-out test set. The test set is balanced (50% positive, 50% negative). What does this score tell you about the model?
options: The model is performing at roughly chance level and is no better than random guessing
The model has learned to perfectly separate the two classes with no errors
The model is performing poorly because it is predicting the wrong class — inverting its predictions would fix it
The model needs more training data; AUC of 0.50 is expected when the training set is too small
explanation:
An AUC of 0.50 on a balanced dataset means the model performs at chance. The ROC curve plots the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate across all classification thresholds. A random classifier — one that assigns scores without regard to the actual class — produces a diagonal line from (0,0) to (1,1), with an area of exactly 0.50. An AUC of 0.50 means the model's ranking of examples is no better than random.

Option B is wrong: perfect separation would produce an AUC of 1.0, meaning the model can rank all positives above all negatives at every threshold.

Option C is a common misconception. If AUC were significantly below 0.50 (e.g. 0.10 or 0.20), inverting predictions would give a high AUC — because the model is consistently wrong, which itself is informative. An AUC of exactly 0.50 means the model has no signal in either direction; inverting would still give 0.50.

Option D is wrong: AUC of 0.50 is not related to training set size as a general rule. A model with access to millions of examples can still achieve 0.50 if the features are uninformative or the model architecture is wrong.
hints: Think about what a diagonal line on the ROC plot represents. What is the model doing at every threshold if its ROC curve is exactly diagonal?
AUC measures the probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative. What does AUC = 0.50 imply about that probability?

title: Loss Function Selection: Regression
description: You are training a regression model to predict delivery times. The training data contains a small number of extreme outliers — packages delayed 10× longer than normal due to exceptional circumstances. Your primary concern is that these outliers do not distort the model's predictions for typical deliveries. Which loss function is most appropriate?
options: Mean Squared Error (MSE) — it is the standard loss function for regression and should always be the default choice
Mean Absolute Error (MAE) — it penalises errors linearly, making it less sensitive to extreme outliers than MSE
Mean Squared Error (MSE) — squaring the errors helps the optimiser distinguish between large and small errors more clearly
Cross-entropy loss — it handles outliers by normalising the error relative to the predicted probability
explanation:
MAE is more robust to outliers because it penalises each error proportionally to its absolute magnitude. MSE squares the error, meaning an outlier with 10× the normal delivery time contributes 100× more to the loss than a typical error. This causes gradient descent to spend disproportionate effort minimising the outlier cases, distorting the model's learned parameters away from what works for typical deliveries.

MAE treats all errors equally in proportion, so outliers have less influence. The model learns to minimise median-like behaviour rather than mean-like behaviour (which is sensitive to extremes).

Option A is wrong: MSE is the default for reasons of mathematical convenience (differentiable, convex), not because it handles outliers well. The choice of loss function should reflect the cost structure of the problem.

Option C is wrong: while squaring does amplify the gradient signal for large errors (helpful in some contexts), it works against you when you specifically want to downweight outliers.

Option D is wrong: cross-entropy is a classification loss, not a regression loss. It operates on probabilities and is not applicable to continuous output prediction.
hints: Compare what squaring does to a 10× error versus a 1× error: the ratio of their squared values is 100. Compare the same ratio for absolute values.
If outliers are not representative of the problem you care about, you want a loss function that does not let them dominate the gradient signal.

title: Loss Function Selection: Classification
description: You are training a neural network to classify customer intent into one of five categories. The output layer has five units. Which loss function is the correct choice for this multi-class problem?
options: Binary cross-entropy with a threshold of 0.5 applied to each output unit independently
Categorical cross-entropy (softmax cross-entropy) — it is designed for mutually exclusive multi-class classification
Mean Squared Error — it works for classification as long as labels are one-hot encoded
Hinge loss — it is the standard loss for any classification task with more than two classes
explanation:
Categorical cross-entropy with a softmax activation is the standard loss for mutually exclusive multi-class classification (where each example belongs to exactly one class). The softmax transforms raw scores into a probability distribution summing to 1 across all classes, and cross-entropy then measures the log-likelihood of the true class.

Option A is wrong: binary cross-entropy is appropriate only for binary classification (one output unit, two classes) or for multi-label classification (where a single example can belong to multiple classes simultaneously). Applying it independently to each unit treats each class as a separate binary decision, which is wrong when classes are mutually exclusive — the outputs won't sum to 1 and each unit can independently output high probability.

Option C is wrong: MSE can technically be applied to one-hot targets, but it does not produce calibrated probability estimates and does not maximise the log-likelihood of the true class. The gradients are also less informative than cross-entropy for classification. MSE is not the right choice here.

Option D is wrong: hinge loss (used in SVMs) is less common for neural network multi-class classification. It does not produce probability outputs and is not the standard for this setup.
hints: Think about what the output layer needs to represent: a probability distribution over five mutually exclusive classes. Which loss function is built for exactly that?
When one of five classes must be the predicted answer (not multiple simultaneously), the loss should enforce that the model's output sums to 1.

title: Decision Tree Splitting Criteria
description: A decision tree algorithm must decide which feature to split on first at the root node. Feature A has a Gini impurity reduction of 0.18 when used for splitting. Feature B has an information gain (entropy reduction) of 0.21. A junior colleague says the choice of Gini vs entropy will determine very different tree structures. Is the colleague correct?
options: Yes — Gini favours binary splits while entropy favours multi-way splits, leading to fundamentally different tree shapes
No — Gini and entropy are monotonically related measures of impurity and almost always select the same feature for splitting in practice
Yes — entropy always produces deeper trees than Gini because log-based calculations penalise pure nodes more heavily
No — both measures produce identical numerical values, so they will always rank features identically
explanation:
In practice, Gini impurity and entropy (information gain) almost always agree on which feature to split. They are both measures of node impurity that reach their minimum at purity (all one class) and their maximum at maximum uncertainty. Because they are monotonically related, they rank features very similarly and produce nearly identical tree structures.

The choice between them is a minor implementation detail. Gini is slightly cheaper to compute (no logarithm), but the resulting trees are not meaningfully different. This is a well-established finding in the decision tree literature.

Option A is wrong: neither Gini nor entropy has a preference for binary vs multi-way splits — that is determined by the algorithm's design (CART always uses binary splits regardless of criterion, while C4.5 uses multi-way splits).

Option C is wrong: tree depth depends on the data and stopping criteria (max depth, min samples per leaf), not on whether Gini or entropy is used as the splitting criterion.

Option D is wrong: Gini and entropy are not numerically identical. They are calculated differently (Gini: 1 - Σp², entropy: -Σp log p), but their rankings of features are almost always the same, which is the practical point.
hints: Consider what both measures are fundamentally trying to do: assess how mixed the classes are in a potential split. Do two different measures of 'mixedness' tend to agree about which feature is most informative?
The key question is whether they rank features differently — not whether they produce the same numbers.

title: Gradient Descent: Learning Rate Effects
description: During training, you observe that the loss curve oscillates wildly, rising and falling between epochs rather than decreasing steadily. The model eventually diverges and the loss becomes NaN. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too low — small steps prevent the optimiser from escaping local minima
The learning rate is too high — large steps cause the optimiser to overshoot minima and bounce around the loss landscape
The batch size is too small — noisy gradient estimates from few examples cause the loss to oscillate
The model architecture is too simple — underfitting causes the loss to be unstable during training
explanation:
Oscillating loss that diverges to NaN is the classic signature of a learning rate that is too high. Gradient descent takes a step in the direction of the negative gradient, scaled by the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large, each step overshoots the minimum of the loss landscape — the model bounces from one side of the valley to the other, getting further away rather than converging. Eventually the parameters blow up to infinity, producing NaN.

Option A is wrong: a learning rate that is too low produces slow but steady convergence — the loss decreases, just very slowly. It does not cause oscillation or divergence.

Option C is wrong: small batch sizes do produce noisy gradient estimates, which can cause some loss fluctuation between steps, but not the violent oscillation and divergence described. Small-batch noise is manageable with an appropriate learning rate.

Option D is wrong: model simplicity (underfitting) causes high but stable loss, not divergence. A linear model on a non-linear problem will plateau at a high loss, not oscillate and diverge.
hints: If the loss is going up and down wildly rather than trending downward, the optimiser is not converging — it is making steps that are too large to land in the right place.
Think of gradient descent as walking downhill. What happens if your steps are too large for the steepness of the terrain?

title: Gradient Descent: Convergence Indicators
description: After 50 training epochs, the training loss has decreased from 2.3 to 1.1 and has been nearly flat for the last 15 epochs. The validation loss mirrors this pattern and is also flat at approximately 1.1. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Stop training — the model has converged and further epochs will only cause overfitting
Increase the learning rate — the flat loss indicates the model is stuck in a local minimum and needs a larger step to escape
Evaluate on the test set immediately — flat validation loss means the model is at its best performance
Investigate model capacity or feature quality — flat, parallel training and validation losses suggest the model may be underfitting
explanation:
When both training and validation loss are flat and approximately equal — especially at a value that is still high — this indicates the model has hit a capacity ceiling, not that it has converged to an optimal solution. The model is underfitting: it lacks the expressive power or the right features to reduce loss further.

The appropriate responses are to increase model complexity (more layers, more features, less regularisation) or to examine feature quality. Simply waiting for more epochs will not help if the gradient signal is gone.

Option A is wrong: stopping is correct only if the model is performing at an acceptable level. If loss = 1.1 is far from your target, stopping wastes the opportunity to improve the model.

Option B is wrong: a flat training loss does not mean a local minimum. If the model were stuck in a sharp local minimum, increasing the learning rate might help it escape — but flat parallel losses with both values still high is the underfitting pattern, not a local minimum.

Option C is wrong: evaluating on the test set should be the final step after all model decisions are made. Using the test set because 'validation is flat' risks leaking test information into model selection decisions.
hints: When training and validation losses are nearly identical and both flat, the gap (overfitting signal) is not the issue — the absolute level is. What does it mean if the model can't push loss lower even on training data?
A model that has truly converged to the best it can do given its capacity is exhibiting underfitting if that best is still far from ideal.

title: Regularisation: L1 vs L2 Effect Direction
description: You have a linear regression model with 200 features, but you suspect that only 20–30 of them are actually relevant. You want the model to automatically identify and discard irrelevant features. Which regularisation approach should you prefer?
options: L2 regularisation (Ridge) — it penalises large weights and will set irrelevant feature weights to exactly zero
L1 regularisation (Lasso) — it produces sparse solutions where coefficients of irrelevant features are driven to exactly zero
L2 regularisation (Ridge) — it distributes weight evenly across correlated features, which is more stable than L1
No regularisation — regularisation only addresses overfitting and is not related to feature selection
explanation:
L1 regularisation (Lasso) adds a penalty proportional to the absolute value of the weights. Geometrically, this creates a constraint region with corners at the coordinate axes, which encourages solutions where many weights are exactly zero. This property — sparsity — makes L1 regularisation a built-in feature selection mechanism.

L2 regularisation (Ridge) adds a penalty proportional to the squared magnitude of weights. Its constraint region is a smooth sphere, which shrinks weights toward zero but rarely to exactly zero. Ridge distributes weight across correlated features and is better for stability when all features are relevant.

Option A is wrong: L2 does not produce zero weights. It produces small weights, but they remain non-zero. This is a fundamental distinction.

Option C is wrong: while L2's property of distributing weight across correlated features is real and valuable, it works against the goal here, which is identifying the 20–30 relevant features.

Option D is wrong: regularisation addresses both overfitting and feature selection. L1 regularisation explicitly selects features by zeroing out uninformative coefficients — this is one of its primary uses.
hints: The key word in the question is 'discard'. Which regularisation method produces coefficients that are exactly zero, effectively removing a feature from the model?
Think about the geometric interpretation: L1's diamond-shaped constraint region has corners that coincide with the axes, encouraging sparse solutions.

title: Regularisation: Diagnosing the Right Remedy
description: A gradient-boosted model achieves 99.2% accuracy on training data and 74.1% on validation data. A colleague proposes increasing the model's max_depth from 6 to 10 to give it more expressive power. What is the correct assessment?
options: The colleague is correct — deeper trees can capture more complex patterns and reduce the validation gap
The model is overfitting and the correct action is regularisation (e.g. reducing max_depth, increasing min_samples_leaf, or adding early stopping), not increasing complexity
The model is underfitting — 74.1% validation accuracy indicates the model lacks capacity, confirming the colleague's suggestion
The colleague is correct — increasing max_depth will reduce training accuracy slightly, which will in turn pull validation accuracy upward
explanation:
The 25-point gap between training (99.2%) and validation (74.1%) accuracy is a clear overfitting signature. The model has memorised the training data. Increasing max_depth makes the model more complex and more capable of memorisation — this will almost certainly make overfitting worse, pushing training accuracy toward 100% while further degrading validation performance.

The correct remedies are to constrain model complexity: shallower trees (lower max_depth), require more samples per leaf (higher min_samples_leaf), increase regularisation (higher lambda/alpha), add early stopping based on validation performance, or increase the number of trees while reducing individual tree depth.

Option A is wrong: more complexity is exactly what an overfitting model does not need. Deeper trees will find more spurious patterns in the training data.

Option C is wrong: underfitting produces similarly poor performance on both training and validation sets. 74.1% validation accuracy with 99.2% training accuracy is not underfitting — it is the exact opposite.

Option D is wrong: reducing training accuracy does not 'pull' validation accuracy upward as a mechanical consequence. Regularisation works by constraining what the model can memorise, not by deliberately degrading training performance.
hints: Before choosing a remedy, correctly diagnose the problem. Is this a case of too little complexity (underfitting) or too much (overfitting)?
The training-validation gap tells you the direction of the problem. Once you know whether you have underfitting or overfitting, the remedy is the opposite of what caused it.

title: Hyperparameter vs Model Parameter
description: After training a logistic regression model, you inspect the learned weights. You find 50 coefficients (one per feature) plus a bias term. Your training script also set max_iter=1000 and C=0.1 before training began. Which items are model parameters and which are hyperparameters?
options: The 50 coefficients and bias term are hyperparameters because they are specific to this training run; max_iter and C are model parameters because they control model behaviour
The 50 coefficients and bias term are model parameters (learned from data); max_iter and C are hyperparameters (set before training)
All four — coefficients, bias, max_iter, and C — are model parameters because they collectively define the model's behaviour on new data
max_iter and C are the only true parameters because they directly affect how the model learns; coefficients are outputs, not parameters
explanation:
Model parameters are values learned from the training data through the optimisation process. For logistic regression, these are the coefficients (weights for each feature) and the bias term — they are the outputs of training and encode everything the model has learned.

Hyperparameters are values set before training begins that control the learning process itself. max_iter caps the number of optimisation iterations; C controls regularisation strength. Neither is learned from data — they are chosen by the practitioner and are fixed during training.

Option A reverses the definitions. The distinction is not about specificity to a training run — it is about whether the value is learned from data or set externally.

Option C is wrong: max_iter and C do not appear in the final model's predictions. They affect how the coefficients are found, but the deployed model only uses the learned coefficients and bias.

Option D is wrong: coefficients are absolutely parameters — they are the quantities that define the model's mapping from input to output. 'Output of training' and 'model parameter' are the same thing.
hints: Ask two questions: (1) Is this value learned by the optimiser during training? (2) Must this value be set before training can begin?
Model parameters live inside the trained model and are used at prediction time. Hyperparameters govern the training process and are no longer needed once training is done.

title: Class Imbalance: When Accuracy Misleads
description: A dataset contains 9,500 legitimate transactions and 500 fraudulent ones (95%/5% split). A model that predicts 'legitimate' for every single transaction achieves 95% accuracy. A colleague concludes this is a good baseline. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing — 95% accuracy is a genuinely strong baseline and any model that cannot beat it on accuracy is not useful
Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data; a model that catches zero fraud has no practical utility, and the correct baseline metric is precision-recall or F1 on the minority class
The colleague is correct that this is a baseline, but accuracy should be computed on a balanced subset of the data to be meaningful
The model predicts correctly 95% of the time, so it must have learned something — the colleague's reasoning is sound
explanation:
When classes are heavily imbalanced, a trivial classifier that always predicts the majority class achieves high accuracy without learning anything. This '95% baseline' is deceptive: it has 0% recall on fraud (the class that matters), 0% precision on fraud, and undefined F1. It is completely useless for its stated purpose.

The correct evaluation metrics for imbalanced classification are precision and recall (or their combination as F1) on the minority class, or AUROC/AUPRC (area under the precision-recall curve, which is more informative than ROC for severe imbalance).

Option A is wrong: 95% accuracy achieved by predicting one class is not a 'strong baseline' — it is a degenerate model. A 'strong baseline' implies the model has actually learned discriminative signal.

Option C is wrong: while computing metrics on a balanced subset can help interpretation, the fundamental problem is using accuracy at all for this problem. The solution is a better metric, not resampling for metric computation.

Option D is wrong: a model that always outputs the same prediction has learned nothing from the features. The 95% accuracy is entirely explained by the class distribution, not by the model's learned representation.
hints: If a model would achieve 95% accuracy by predicting the same thing for every example regardless of the input features, what does that tell you about the metric's ability to detect whether the model has actually learned anything?
Think about what the fraud detection system's actual job is: catching fraud. What is the model's performance at that specific task?

title: Cross-Validation: Stratified K-Fold
description: You have a binary classification dataset where 8% of examples are positive. You apply standard k-fold cross-validation (without stratification). A colleague warns this could be problematic. In which scenario would the colleague's concern be most valid?
options: When k is large (e.g. k=10), because smaller validation sets have higher variance regardless of class distribution
When the dataset is small, because a random fold might contain very few or zero positive examples, making the fold's evaluation uninformative or undefined
When the model is a decision tree, because trees are more sensitive to class imbalance than linear models
When features are correlated, because stratification is primarily designed to handle multicollinearity
explanation:
With only 8% positive examples, a small dataset might have as few as 40 positives in 500 examples. A random fold for k=5 would contain about 100 examples, of which roughly 8 should be positive. By chance, a fold might contain 0, 1, or 2 positives — making metrics like precision, recall, and F1 undefined or highly unstable.

Stratified k-fold ensures each fold contains approximately the same class proportion as the full dataset. For an 8% positive rate, each fold will contain ~8% positives by design.

Option A is wrong: higher k does increase variance in fold estimates, but that is independent of the class imbalance problem. The concern about empty or near-empty minority classes is most acute with small datasets, not necessarily large k.

Option C is wrong: trees and linear models can both be affected by class imbalance in cross-validation. The model type does not change whether folds have representative class distributions.

Option D is wrong: stratification refers to maintaining class distribution across folds — it has nothing to do with feature correlation or multicollinearity.
hints: With only 8% positive examples and a small dataset, calculate roughly how many positives you would expect in a random fold. What happens to metrics if that number is 0 or 1?
Stratification solves a representativeness problem: each fold should look like a miniature version of the full dataset in terms of class distribution.

title: Regression Metrics: MSE vs MAE
description: Two models predict apartment rental prices. Model A has MAE = $180 and MSE = 180,000. Model B has MAE = $220 and MSE = 38,000. A product manager cares about the typical error a user experiences when the model's estimate differs from the actual rent. Which model does the product manager prefer, and why?
options: Model A — it has lower MAE, meaning the typical error experienced by users is smaller
Model B — it has lower MSE, meaning it avoids large individual errors that would be noticed by users
Model A — lower MSE always reflects better real-world performance regardless of MAE
Model B — lower MAE indicates fewer total errors even though individual errors can be larger
explanation:
MAE (Mean Absolute Error) measures the average absolute error across all predictions — it is the average deviation a user experiences. The product manager cares about 'the typical error', which is precisely what MAE measures.

Model A's MAE of $180 means users, on average, see a $180 discrepancy between the estimate and actual rent. Model B's MAE of $220 means the typical discrepancy is $220. From the product manager's perspective, Model A provides a better user experience on average.

Model B's lower MSE means it has fewer very large individual errors — MSE amplifies large errors due to squaring. Model B might be preferred by an engineer who wants to avoid rare extreme mispredictions (e.g. being off by $2,000 on a single listing), but that is a different objective from minimising typical user-facing error.

Option B is wrong for the product manager's stated preference. They want to minimise the typical experience, not the worst cases.

Option C is wrong: lower MSE does not 'always' reflect better real-world performance. It reflects better performance on a squared-error objective, which penalises outliers more. The right metric depends on what the business cares about.

Option D is wrong: lower MAE does not mean fewer total errors. It means the average error is smaller. A model could have fewer errors overall but larger ones, producing a higher MAE.
hints: The product manager used the word 'typical'. Which metric directly measures the average (typical) deviation across all predictions?
MAE and MSE can rank models differently when one model has smaller average errors but occasional large ones. Identify which model fits that profile.

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Diagnosing from Curves
description: You plot learning curves for a model: as training set size increases from 1,000 to 50,000 examples, training accuracy decreases slightly from 96% to 91%, and validation accuracy increases slightly from 65% to 72%. After 50,000 examples, both curves have stabilised and stopped moving. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: The model needs more training data — the validation curve has not yet reached training accuracy
The model is converging correctly and more data will eventually close the training-validation gap
The model has high variance (overfitting) — adding more features would help it capture the underlying pattern better
The model has high bias — the stabilised gap and low absolute validation accuracy suggest the model lacks capacity, and more data alone will not close the gap
explanation:
The pattern of stabilised, parallel learning curves with a persistent gap indicates high bias (underfitting). A high-bias model has insufficient capacity to represent the true relationship. Adding more training data to an underfitting model produces diminishing returns — the curves converge to a stable gap that more data cannot close.

This is the diagnostic signature: both curves stop improving, the gap remains, and validation accuracy plateaus well below an acceptable level. The remedy is to increase model capacity: more features, a richer feature representation, a more complex model architecture, or less regularisation.

Option A is wrong: adding more data to a model with stabilised learning curves will not help. The curves have plateaued — the bottleneck is model capacity, not data volume.

Option B is wrong: the model is not 'converging correctly'. Correct convergence means validation approaches training accuracy. Here they stabilise at different levels.

Option C is wrong: high variance (overfitting) would show a large gap that shrinks as training data increases — the model needs data to reduce memorisation. Here the gap does not shrink with more data, ruling out variance as the primary issue. Also, more features would make overfitting worse, not better.
hints: When learning curves stabilise and stop improving with more data, the bottleneck is no longer data volume. What else determines how well a model can fit the data?
High-bias and high-variance models produce different shapes of learning curves. In the high-bias case, what happens to the gap between training and validation as data increases?

title: Data Splitting: Leakage from Preprocessing
description: Before splitting data, a team imputes missing values using the mean of the entire dataset, then splits into train/validation/test sets. A colleague flags this as problematic. What is the issue?
options: There is no issue — imputing before splitting is standard practice and avoids inconsistency between train and validation imputation statistics
The validation and test set statistics (means) have leaked into the training set imputation, producing an optimistically biased estimate of generalisation performance
The training set statistics have leaked into the validation and test sets, biasing the performance estimate optimistically because the model has indirect knowledge of those sets
Imputation should never be done before splitting, because it changes the feature distribution and makes the train/test distributions different
explanation:
Imputing before splitting causes data leakage in the direction of training set contamination of the validation/test sets. When the mean is computed over the entire dataset, it incorporates information from the validation and test examples. The model is then trained on data where the imputed values reflect statistics from the held-out sets — the model has indirect access to information it should not have seen.

In production, you would compute imputation statistics on the training set only and apply them to new data. Imputing before splitting simulates a situation where future data has already been seen, producing an optimistic bias in the estimated performance.

Option A is wrong: while consistency is a real goal, the correct way to achieve it is to fit the imputer on training data and transform all sets with those same training statistics.

Option B is wrong in the direction of the leak. It is the training set that benefits from knowing validation/test statistics, not the other way around.

Option D is wrong: the concern is not about distribution differences. The concern is that the held-out sets' information influences what is learned during training, invalidating the independence assumption of the evaluation.
hints: Think about what the mean-based imputation computes: a statistic over the entire dataset. Which rows' data is included in that statistic?
In deployment, you can only use statistics computed from data seen before the model is trained. Does imputing before splitting respect that constraint?

title: Hyperparameter vs Parameter: Neural Networks
description: A neural network is trained with the following configuration: learning_rate=0.001, hidden_layers=3, units_per_layer=128, dropout_rate=0.2. After training, the network has 2.4 million weight values. A new engineer asks which of these are 'the model'. What is the correct answer?
options: The configuration values (learning_rate, hidden_layers, units_per_layer, dropout_rate) are the model — they define its structure
The 2.4 million weight values are the model — they are what is saved, loaded, and used to make predictions on new data
Both the configuration and the weights are the model — removing either makes the network unable to make predictions
The model is defined by hidden_layers and units_per_layer only — these determine the architecture; weights and learning_rate are auxiliary
explanation:
The 2.4 million weight values are the model — they are what is learned during training and what encodes the model's knowledge. When you save a trained model and deploy it, you are saving and loading these weights. They are applied at inference time to transform inputs into predictions.

The configuration values (learning_rate, dropout_rate, etc.) are hyperparameters that governed the training process. After training completes, learning_rate and dropout_rate (used only during training) are no longer needed for inference. hidden_layers and units_per_layer define the architecture (how many weights there are) but are not themselves the learned values.

Option A is wrong: the configuration defines the training setup and architecture, but it is not 'the model' in the sense of what was learned. Two models with the same configuration but different random initialisations will have completely different weights.

Option C is partially true — you need the architecture specification to load the weights correctly — but the statement that 'removing either makes the network unable to make predictions' conflates the architecture blueprint (needed to interpret weights) with the weights themselves (the actual knowledge).

Option D is wrong: learning_rate and dropout_rate are not 'auxiliary'; they are hyperparameters that directly shape which weights are found during training. But the weights, not the hyperparameters, are what constitute the deployable model.
hints: Ask: which of these values are saved to disk when you call 'model.save()'? Which are used when you call 'model.predict(new_data)'?
The model's knowledge is encoded in the values that were adjusted by the optimiser during training to minimise the loss.

title: Feature Scaling: SVM and Neural Networks
description: You are building a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to classify customer segments. Your features include account age (1–10 years), number of transactions (0–5,000), and a binary flag (0 or 1). Without scaling, you run the SVM and get poor performance. A colleague suggests scaling is the issue. Are they right?
options: No — SVMs are kernel-based and the kernel computation makes them inherently scale-invariant
Yes — SVMs rely on distance-based margin maximisation; features with larger scale dominate the margin calculation and distort the decision boundary
No — the binary flag (0 or 1) will anchor the feature space and prevent scale issues in the other features
Yes — but only if using a non-linear kernel; linear SVMs are scale-invariant by definition
explanation:
SVMs are fundamentally scale-sensitive because they work by finding the maximum-margin hyperplane between classes. The margin is measured in the feature space using Euclidean distance. A feature with range 0–5,000 contributes millions of times more to the distance calculation than a binary 0/1 feature, effectively making the SVM's decision depend almost entirely on the transaction count feature while ignoring the others.

The RBF (Gaussian) kernel, which computes distances between points, is also scale-dependent. Feature scaling is essential for SVMs with any kernel that uses distance.

Option A is wrong: kernels transform the feature space but still operate on distances or dot products. Scale differences in the original feature space are preserved through most kernel computations (including RBF and polynomial).

Option C is wrong: the binary flag being bounded does not 'anchor' anything — the large-scale features still dominate the margin calculation.

Option D is wrong: linear SVMs also use distance-based margin maximisation and are equally sensitive to feature scale. The scale invariance claim for linear SVMs is incorrect.
hints: SVMs find the hyperplane that maximises margin — margin is a distance in feature space. What happens to a distance-based calculation when one feature has values 100× larger than another?
The same reasoning that makes KNN sensitive to scale applies to any algorithm that uses distances between data points.

title: Cross-Validation: Correct Usage with Test Set
description: A team uses 5-fold cross-validation to select the best model from 10 candidates and then reports the average cross-validation score as the model's final performance. What is the problem with this approach?
options: 5-fold cross-validation is too few folds — at least 10 folds are needed to produce a reliable estimate after model selection
The cross-validation score is biased upward because it was used for model selection, not just estimation — a separate held-out test set should be used for the final reported number
There is no problem — cross-validation produces an unbiased estimate regardless of how many models were compared
The problem is that 10 candidate models were evaluated — cross-validation is only valid when comparing 2–3 models
explanation:
When cross-validation is used both to select the best model and to report its performance, the reported score is optimistically biased. By picking the model with the best CV score from 10 candidates, you are selecting the one that got 'lucky' on the folds — exploiting random variation in the fold assignments. The winner's score is not an unbiased estimate of its true generalisation error.

The correct procedure is: use cross-validation for model selection, then evaluate the final selected model on a completely separate test set that was never involved in selection. That test set score is the unbiased final estimate.

Option A is wrong: the number of folds affects the estimate's variance but not the fundamental bias introduced by using the same CV for selection and reporting.

Option C is wrong: cross-validation provides an unbiased estimate only if it is not also used as the selection criterion. When it drives selection, the selected model's CV score is biased upward.

Option D is wrong: there is no constraint on how many models can be compared. The issue is the reporting methodology, not the number of candidates.
hints: Think about what 'selecting the best from 10 candidates' does to the expected CV score of the winner. Are you guaranteed to pick the model with the best true performance, or might you sometimes pick a model that got lucky?
The same folds that selected the model cannot be used to fairly evaluate it — there is an analogy to evaluating on the validation set you used for hyperparameter tuning.

title: Classification Metrics: F1 Score
description: A model for detecting defective products has precision = 0.60 and recall = 0.90. The factory's quality team says catching every defect is critical — missing a defect reaches the customer. The production team says false alarms are expensive — each false positive means halting the line unnecessarily. A manager asks for a single metric that captures both concerns equally. What do you report, and what is its approximate value?
options: Accuracy — it naturally balances precision and recall for binary problems; approximately 75%
F1 score — the harmonic mean of precision and recall; approximately 0.72
F1 score — the arithmetic mean of precision and recall; approximately 0.75
Recall — the manager said catching defects is 'critical', so recall is the only metric that matters; 0.90
explanation:
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F1 = 2 × (precision × recall) / (precision + recall) = 2 × (0.60 × 0.90) / (0.60 + 0.90) = 2 × 0.54 / 1.50 = 1.08 / 1.50 ≈ 0.72.

The harmonic mean is used (rather than arithmetic) because it penalises large imbalances between precision and recall more heavily. A model with precision=0.10 and recall=0.99 would have an arithmetic mean of ~0.55 but an F1 of only ~0.18, reflecting that the precision is unacceptably low.

Option A is wrong: accuracy is a poor summary metric when precision and recall are both relevant because it depends on class distribution. High recall and moderate precision can coexist with misleadingly high accuracy if the negative class dominates.

Option C is wrong: the arithmetic mean (0.75) overstates performance compared to the harmonic mean. It does not penalise the imbalance between 0.60 and 0.90 as strongly as the harmonic mean does.

Option D is wrong: the manager explicitly asked for a metric that captures both concerns equally. Reporting recall alone ignores the production team's constraint about false alarms.
hints: The F1 score formula is the harmonic mean: 2 × (P × R) / (P + R). Try computing it directly.
The harmonic mean is chosen over the arithmetic mean specifically because it penalises large gaps between precision and recall — a model that is great on one but terrible on the other gets a low F1.

title: Regularisation: Effect on Model Complexity
description: A neural network trained without regularisation achieves 98% training accuracy and 73% validation accuracy. You add L2 regularisation and retrain. The result is 89% training accuracy and 84% validation accuracy. A colleague is concerned that the training accuracy dropped and argues the regularised model is worse. How do you respond?
options: The colleague is correct — training accuracy is the best indicator of model quality because it reflects how much the model has learned from the data
The regularised model is better — the goal is to maximise validation performance, which improved from 73% to 84%; the drop in training accuracy is expected and desirable
Both models are equally good — you should average the training and validation accuracy for a fair comparison
The colleague is correct — you should lower the regularisation strength until training accuracy recovers to 98%
explanation:
The regularised model is better. The goal of training an ML model is not to maximise performance on the training set — it is to generalise to unseen data. Validation accuracy is the proxy for generalisation, and it improved from 73% to 84%.

Regularisation works precisely by constraining the model from perfectly fitting the training data. The drop in training accuracy from 98% to 89% is the expected trade-off: the model is less overfit, which means it captures the underlying signal rather than training-set noise. This allows it to generalise better.

Option A is wrong: training accuracy measures how well the model has memorised the training data, not how well it has learned to generalise. High training accuracy with low validation accuracy is the hallmark of a poor model in deployment.

Option C is wrong: averaging training and validation accuracy is not a standard or meaningful metric. These measure fundamentally different things.

Option D is wrong: recovering training accuracy to 98% would undo the regularisation benefit and return the model to its overfitting state with 73% validation accuracy. The goal is the best validation performance, not the highest training performance.
hints: What is the model ultimately for — to perform well on data it has already seen, or on data it will encounter in the future?

Regularisation intentionally introduces a constraint that accepts slightly worse training performance in exchange for better generalisation. Is 'better generalisation' reflected in training or validation accuracy?
